topic.title: No Cost EMI
topic.claim: No Cost EMI moves the cost to a column you don't read, and what sellers really buy is your comparison.
topic.moment: The green 'No Cost EMI' line under the price at checkout in the festive sale.

turn.actually: the interest is still charged and offset by a discount; GST on the interest, fees and lost discounts remain

topic.because: the brand, platform or bank funds the interest because EMI makes more people buy, and buy bigger; a monthly number gets compared to a salary, not to other phones
topic.payoff: When a price gets broken into months, the full number was losing the argument.

proof.fact: Redseer estimated about Rs 24,000 crore of sales in the first two days of the 2026 online festive sales, with mobiles 38-40%
iPhone 17 256GB listed at Rs 86,999 on Flipkart in Big Billion Days 2026, with a six-month no-cost EMI
With card no-cost EMI the bank charges interest and the seller gives an equal discount; 18% GST applies to the interest; processing fees and foreclosure charges may apply

paragraphs: Nobody gives you a free loan in a festive sale. "No Cost EMI" just moves the cost to a column you don't read.
slides.why_swipe: a claim that the line everyone trusts hides something; which column?

paragraphs: iPhone 17, 256GB. ₹86,999 in Big Billion Days earlier this month. Right under it: No Cost EMI.
slides.why_swipe: the reader feels the switch in their own head; how is it no cost?

paragraphs: On most card EMIs, the bank still charges interest. The seller knocks the same amount off the price upfront. Net zero, on paper.
Off paper, your card statement often shows 18% GST on that interest, and many banks add a processing fee.
slides.why_swipe: the costs are out; why would anyone pay your interest?

paragraphs: Ask anyone on the selling side: it isn't charity. The brand, the platform or the bank pays that interest because EMI makes more people buy, and buy bigger.
slides.why_swipe: the scale explains the motive; what is the money buying?

big.label: online festive sales in the first two days; phones nearly 40%

paragraphs: What they're paying for is how the price feels.
₹86,999 feels like a decision. ₹14,500 feels like one more monthly bill, and next to a salary almost any monthly bill looks small.
**When a price gets broken into months, the full number was losing the argument.**
slides.why_swipe: the idea has landed; the last slide makes it personal

paragraphs: Someone is reading this right now on a phone with four payments left.

draft.caption: What's the most expensive thing you bought because the monthly number looked small?
draft.alt_text: A text carousel explaining that No Cost EMI still carries interest offset by a discount, GST on that interest and fees, and that sellers fund it because a monthly figure gets compared to a salary rather than to other phones.
